identity.title: mCLM: A Modular Chemical Language Model that Generates Functional and Makeable Molecules

problem.claim: Enable LLMs to generate small molecules with desired functions that are also compatible with automated synthesis.

gap.claim: Existing molecule LLMs represent molecules at the atom level, limiting functional and synthesis-aware generation.

contributions.claim: Proposes mCLM, a modular chemical-language model using functional building blocks and a bilingual model for natural-language function descriptions and molecular blocks.
Front-loads synthesizability considerations while aiming to improve predicted molecular functions.
Reports improvements in molecular function, synthetic accessibility, and property scores across in-distribution and out-of-distribution medicine settings.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish mCLM through functional-building-block tokenization, analogous to meaning-bearing subword tokenization, and modular synthesis alignment.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments on 430 FDA-approved drugs significantly improved chemical functions relevant to drug potential.
The authors report that the 3B-parameter mCLM improved synthetic accessibility relative to seven other generative AI methods, including GPT-5.

On 122 out-of-distribution medicines restricted to blocks compatible with automated modular synthesis, the authors report that mCLM outperformed all baselines in property scores and synthetic accessibility; they also report multi-function reasoning and iterative self-improvement for failed clinical candidates.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs understand chemical knowledge but struggle to propose functional molecules that are practical to synthesize.
The paper argues for a new molecular language based on functional building blocks rather than atoms, aligned with automated synthesis.
mCLM combines modular molecular blocks with natural-language function descriptions and incorporates synthesizability early.
Experiments report gains on approved drugs, competing generative methods, out-of-distribution medicines, and iterative rescue of failed candidates.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects a representational change—functional-block tokenization—to both molecular function prediction and synthesis compatibility.

lessons.interpretation: A domain-specific representation can make a model's output constraints explicit while linking them to the target objective.
lessons.application: When proposing a generative scientific model, define units that jointly encode task-relevant semantics and downstream feasibility, then align the architecture with both.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when atomic-level detail is itself essential or no stable functional decomposition exists.

unknowns: The abstract gives no numerical effect sizes, statistical details, datasets beyond the stated drug counts, or evaluation protocols.
The seven baselines are not individually identified, and the basis of the reported outperformance is unspecified.
The mechanism and evidence for iterative rescue of “fallen angels” are not detailed.
